items.excerpt: Publishers are still waiting for 'clear' legal answers on AI training, outputs and licensing, the Publishers' Licensing Services (PLS) Conference heard, with key questions for publishers' AI strategies still unresolved by ongoing copyright litigation.

Michael Caine has licensed an AI-generated version of his voice to narrate an audiobook adaptation of Homer's Odyssey, produced with voice-AI company ElevenLabs — a marquee case of a major actor formally licensing, rather than fighting, an AI voice clone for a literary work.

More than 250 UK publishers have opted in to Publishers' Licensing Services' collective AI licensing scheme, which lets publishers jointly manage and monetize licensing of their content to AI companies — a concrete counter-model to unlicensed scraping.

Library ebook-lending app Libby will let readers filter out AI-narrated and AI-written titles — but the filters rely on AI content being self-labeled by publishers, raising questions about how effective the screening can really be.

Writer Jamir Nazir won the Commonwealth Short Story Prize despite earlier accusations of AI use; the Commonwealth Foundation cleared him after a month-long investigation that notably did not use AI-detection software, while Granta ended its partnership with the prize over 'editorial integrity' concerns.

US AI companies are reportedly buying large quantities of secondhand books in German-speaking markets — scanning then destroying them — to train language models, while an Australian survey finds 17.4% of audiobook listeners have already tried AI narration.

Jane Friedman's industry roundup flags the rise of ChatGPT 'infinite story demanders' — readers generating large volumes of personalized AI fanfiction and erotica for private consumption — alongside shifts in book discovery and author platform economics.
Book Riot's weekly news roundup leads with the writer accused of AI use who went on to win the Commonwealth Prize, alongside the week's other publishing developments.

Fiction-writing tool Sudowrite added Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 5 as a writing model in its June 30 update, alongside folder exports and keyboard-accessible document reordering — a fresh model upgrade for AI-assisted novelists. (Off-list domain: official Sudowrite changelog for keyword 'Sudowrite'; no allowed-domain outlet covered this release. Date from on-page changelog entry date.)

Kobo CEO Michael Tamblyn says features coming in fall/winter 2026 will 'fundamentally change how we read and write' on its e-readers, with summer updates including StoryGraph integration and a revamped Web Reader — signaling Kobo's next AI-era reading platform push.
